A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RUPTA work, with matching core methods, datasets and experiments. Their text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial expansion and reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original anonymization and occupation-classification results in Tables 2–3, optimization analyses in Figures 3–4, and distillation experiments in Figures 5–6.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds human evaluation, computational measurements, adapted-method experiments and further sensitivity and control results.

M1.justification: The core evaluators, lexicographic optimization loop and distillation approach remain. Appendix B adds implemented variants that adapt DEID-GPT and SD as RUPTA optimizers by appending prompts conditioning anonymization on privacy and utility feedback. This is a limited procedural extension.

E1.justification: Both versions use DB-bio celebrity biographies and PersonalReddit comments, preserving occupation classification while obscuring personal information. The added human ratings and appendix experiments assess this retained coverage; they introduce no new domain or downstream task.

E2.justification: v2 retains Azure, DEID-GPT, SD and AF, adding IncogniText to both main comparisons. Table 6 adds adapted DEID-GPT and SD variants, and Table 10 adds untuned Phi-3 and Llama-3 controls. These are limited extensions to the existing comparison families.

E3.justification: v2 substantially broadens evaluation procedures: 100 randomly selected DB-bio examples receive meaning-preservation and fluency ratings from three non-authors on five-point scales; appendices add runtime/token measurements, joint threshold/iteration settings and validation/test comparisons. The stated minimum biography length changes from 300 to 200 words, although split counts and original results remain unchanged; rerunning those experiments is not established.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained optimization curves and distillation case study, v2 adds feedback-transfer experiments, joint K/T sensitivity, validation/test consistency and untuned-model controls in Appendices B, C and E. Human evaluation and computational analysis additionally examine semantic loss, fluency and practical expense, substantially expanding the questions investigated.

E5.justification: v2 introduces one-tailed paired t-tests against AF in Tables 1–2 and reports five-run averages for the validation/test experiment. v1 provides neither disclosure; an increased run count for the original experiments is not established. Table 1 incorrectly marks RUPTA's CS as significantly better despite 53.11 exceeding AF's 50.84 under a lower-is-better metric.

E6.justification: The original main-table scores are retained, but substantial new results cover IncogniText, human ratings, costs, method transfer, sensitivity and controls. For example, IncogniText obtains DB-bio SR 58.06 and accuracy 88.28; human semantic-preservation/fluency scores are 3.96/3.68 for RUPTA versus 3.78/3.71 for AF. Table 10 redisplays existing SFT/DPO results from Figure 5; its untuned-model rows are new.

T1.justification: Equations 1–6, the privacy-first lexicographic ordering and the mathematical reasoning are retained. Algorithm input labels and an undefined memory-tuple symbol are corrected without substantively changing the formulation. Neither version supplies a formal privacy proof.

C1.justification: The introduction's novelty claim shifts from first simultaneously optimizing privacy and utility with LLMs to first providing comprehensive studies of anonymization and utility in this setting. v2 emphasizes module studies and presents distillation more as an investigation. The central framework, dataset and comparative-performance claims remain.

C2.justification: Appendix D adds a memorization-based threat-model rationale and characterizes celebrity evaluation as an upper bound on attack success. Appendix F adds an explanation connecting classifier degradation to distribution mismatch and defends the utility metrics. New interpretations attribute IncogniText's utility loss to synthetic distraction and RUPTA's semantic preservation to passage-level processing. The earlier limitations remain.

D1.justification: Appendix G.1 newly specifies main-experiment T=5, K=10, Azure API version and GPT model versions. Existing fine-tuning hyperparameters and hardware are largely retained, but v1's statement about initializing DPO from the best SFT checkpoint is omitted. The repository reference changes, and code/data availability wording shifts from available to future release.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially expands positioning against differential-privacy and representation-learning approaches and discusses the development of LLM anonymization, including IncogniText. Additional citations motivate occupation classification and Wikipedia-based evaluation. The earlier detailed related-work appendix is retained as Appendix H, so that relocation itself is not an addition.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, method explanations and results discussion undergo extensive rewriting. Section 5.5 adds a human-evaluation narrative, and the appendix organization expands from A–D to A–H while relocating existing material. These changes substantially revise the document's exposition and structure.

P2.justification: v2 adds tables displaying human ratings, utility trajectories, costs, transferred methods, validation/test results, joint sensitivity and distillation controls. It relocates dataset statistics, expands Figure 2's caption and adds frames around appendix prompt figures. Existing result plots and anonymization examples remain, with changes to placement and sizing.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the paper's central benefits: human ratings assess meaning and fluency beyond classifier accuracy, while adapted-method and untuned-model controls better establish the contributions of feedback and distillation. Cost measurements and explicit main-experiment settings improve practical assessment and reproducibility. These gains outweigh localized reporting problems, especially the contradictory CS significance annotation and unexplained preprocessing revision; the original benchmark scores themselves remain unchanged.
